title: One in Three Indian Employees in Their 30s Has Elevated Blood Sugar
excerpt: Loop Health's Workforce Health Index 2026, built on 816,000+ lab values, found blood-sugar dysfunction rising from 16.7% in employees' 20s to 52.9% in their 40s — with most people unaware anything is wrong.
body:
• Loop Health's Workforce Health Index 2026 found that 33% of employees in their 30s show blood-sugar dysfunction based on HbA1c results — rising from 16.7% in their 20s to 52.9% in their 40s.
  • The report, built on 816,000+ lab values from urban working Indians, also found widespread deficiencies: 81.4% of employees below the Vitamin D sufficiency threshold and 73.9% low on Vitamin B12.
  • Only 5.8% of respondents said they had been diagnosed with diabetes — far below the 38.7% showing blood-sugar dysfunction across the full tested group.
  • Co-founder Ryan Singh: "One in three professionals in their 30s already shows blood-sugar dysfunction, and that is only one part of the picture."

One in three Indian professionals in their 30s already shows blood-sugar dysfunction, according to a new national assessment of the country's urban workforce — a finding that puts India's metabolic-health warning decade squarely in the prime working years.

Loop Health has released the second edition of its Workforce Health Index (WHI) 2026, a national assessment of urban workforce health built on more than 816,000 lab values across 11,400+ health reports and 9,000+ survey responses, plus 74,000+ hospital claims

The headline finding: glucose dysfunction stood at 31.3% among employees tested in 2026, and the share climbs sharply with age — from 16.7% among employees in their 20s to 33% among those in their 30s and 52.9% in their 40s, based on HbA1c results. Across the full tested group of employees and dependents, 38.7% flagged blood-sugar dysfunction, while only 5.8% of survey respondents said they had ever been diagnosed with diabetes — a gap between measured markers and self-reported diagnoses that the report flags as a call for routine testing.

"The most important finding from WHI 2026 is how early these health risks are showing up. One in three professionals in their 30s already shows blood-sugar dysfunction, and that is only one part of the picture."

— Ryan Singh, Co-Founder and COO, Loop Health

Context & Background

The blood-sugar finding is part of a wider picture of lifestyle disease arriving early. The index also found nutritional deficiencies at striking scale: 81.4% of Vitamin D reports were below the sufficiency threshold (with 60.1% deficient or severely deficient), and 73.9% of employee reports recorded low Vitamin B12 levels. Anaemia was another significant finding — 34.6% of female reports had haemoglobin below 12 g/dL, with the share rising from 30.6% in the 20–29 age group to 37.5% in the 40–49 group.

The gender split in the blood-sugar data is also telling. Among employees in their 30s, 10.3% of men and 4.3% of women fell into the diabetic-range category — a reminder that the dysfunction underway is not evenly distributed. The 2025 edition had already found 37.2% of professionals with abnormal glucose metabolism; the larger 2026 sample shows core health risks have stayed stubbornly high, with a few lifestyle indicators moving in the wrong direction.

Impact & Analysis

What makes the WHI data unsettling is not just the numbers but the silence around them. The vast majority of people flagging blood-sugar dysfunction do not know it: only a fraction have a diabetes diagnosis, meaning these signals are visible in bloodwork well before anyone feels unwell. HbA1c reflects average blood sugar over two to three months, so a dysfunction flag is not a one-off reading — it is a sustained pattern.

The report's own co-founder framed the gap as the core challenge: "Most of these signals are visible well before someone feels unwell. That is where prevention has to start — with knowing what is happening, getting the right medical guidance and acting before a health problem becomes a much bigger one."

There is a caveat worth noting: WHI 2026 draws on Loop Health's own customer base — urban, insured, working Indians — so it is not a nationally representative sample. But as a window into the office-going population, it is one of the largest datasets of its kind, and its direction of travel matches other recent findings, including Apollo Hospitals' Health of Nation Report, which has flagged rising pre-diabetes among young Indians.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the report is a double prompt. First, a practical one: South Asians face elevated diabetes risk at lower body weights than other populations, so an annual HbA1c check in the 30s is not overcautious — it is the baseline. Second, a family one: many diaspora readers have parents and siblings in India in precisely the urban-workforce cohort this report covers, and forwarding a health report can be easier than nagging about checkups.

What's Next

For readers, the actionable takeaway is simple: get an annual health check that includes HbA1c, Vitamin D and B12, and act on the numbers before symptoms force the issue. With 33% of 30-somethings already flagging dysfunction, the odds say someone on every office floor already has it.
